messages.content: Write a post about why a company is investing in developer relations. Around 250 words.

**Why we're hiring a devrel team**

We shipped [product] eighteen months ago and then watched something we didn't like. People signed up. They read the quickstart, got a hello-world running, and then stopped. About [X]% never made a second API call.

We assumed the docs were the problem. In places they were. But the actual issue surfaced when [name] sat with five customers and watched them build. All five stalled in the same spot: [specific step]. Not because it's difficult, but because nobody had written down the part where you wire it into a real system, with real auth, and data that isn't clean.

You can't fix that with marketing, and a webinar won't touch it. It's a craft problem. It needs people whose job is to build with the thing in public, run into the walls, and then go repair the walls.

So we're funding a devrel team of [N], reporting into [engineering/product] rather than marketing. Their mandate: ship reference implementations, answer in the [Discord/forum] inside a day, and file bugs against our own onboarding that carry the same weight as customer bugs. We'll judge them on time-to-second-call and on how many docs PRs land — not on conference talks or follower counts.

Put plainly: we built something developers can use, then left them to work out the hard parts alone. This is us paying that back.

[Roles are open here.]

**Why we're funding a devrel team**

[product] shipped eighteen months ago. Signups came in. People read the quickstart, got hello-world running, and then went quiet. Roughly [X]% never made a second API call.

Our first theory was the docs. Some of that held up. But the real answer came when [name] sat down with five customers and watched them build. All five stopped at [specific step]. It isn't a hard step. Nobody had ever written up the part where you connect it to a system that already exists, with real auth and data that came from somewhere messy.

Marketing can't fix that. Neither can a webinar. It's a craft problem, and craft problems need people whose job is to build with the thing in public, hit the walls, and then go fix the walls.

So we're funding a devrel team of [N], reporting to [engineering/product] rather than marketing. We're asking them to ship reference implementations, answer in the [Discord/forum] within a day, and file bugs against our own onboarding that get triaged like customer bugs. We'll measure time-to-second-call and docs PRs merged, not talks given or followers gained.

The honest version is that we built something developers can use and then left them alone for the hard part. We're paying that back.

[Open roles here.]
